document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 58-year-old man reports six months of progressively muffled hearing in the right ear, with no pain and no discharge. Both external canals are clear of cerumen on otoscopy. A 512 Hz tuning fork placed on the vertex of the skull is heard louder in the right ear. When the same fork is held firmly on the right mastoid and then held beside the right pinna, he says it is louder on the mastoid. Which interpretation of these findings is most likely correct?

options.text: Symmetric hearing thresholds in both ears

questions.explanation: Weber lateralization indicates either ipsilateral conductive hearing loss or contralateral sensorineural hearing loss. Bone conduction louder than air conduction is a negative (abnormal) Rinne, which indicates conductive loss in the tested ear. Weber lateralizing to the right plus a negative Rinne on the right therefore localizes a conductive loss to the right ear; the clear canals mean the result is not an artifact of cerumen.

optionExplanations.b: A right sensorineural loss would make the Weber lateralize to the left, and the Rinne on the right would remain positive (AC>BC).
optionExplanations.c: A left conductive loss would lateralize the Weber to the left and give a negative Rinne on the left, not the right.
optionExplanations.d: A left sensorineural loss lateralizes the Weber to the right, but the right Rinne would be positive rather than negative.
optionExplanations.e: With symmetric hearing the Weber stays central and the Rinne is positive bilaterally; the Weber only lateralizes when the interaural difference exceeds about 6 dB.

questions.topic: Tuning Fork Tests and Types of Hearing Loss

source.reference: OT9 — Auditory Acuity (Rinne and Weber Tests)

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman describes recurrent attacks of spinning lasting less than a minute, brought on by rolling over in bed or tipping her head back to have her hair washed. She denies hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness, and her neurological examination is normal. Moving her rapidly from sitting to supine with the head turned 45 degrees to the right and the neck extended reproduces vertigo with rotatory nystagmus after a short latency. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo consists of acute attacks of transient rotatory vertigo lasting less than one minute, initiated by certain head positions and accompanied by torsional nystagmus. A positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver, with vertigo and rotatory nystagmus appearing after a latency of roughly 20 seconds, confirms the diagnosis on the dependent side. This patient's positional trigger, brief duration, absence of auditory symptoms, and positive Dix-Hallpike are all characteristic.

optionExplanations.b: Meniere's disease produces episodes lasting minutes to hours with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness, none of which are present.
optionExplanations.c: Vestibular neuronitis causes severe continuous vertigo lasting one to five days, not repeated attacks of under a minute triggered by position.
optionExplanations.d: Vestibular schwannoma typically presents with chronic progressive unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus; true vertigo is rare because the tumour grows slowly enough to allow compensation.
optionExplanations.e: Cerebellar infarction causes prolonged vertigo with neurological signs and is suspected mainly in patients with vascular risk factors; the examination here is normal.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man develops severe pain in the right pinna and right side of the face. Four days later a crop of vesicles erupts on the right pinna and in the right external auditory canal. He now has complete weakness of all muscle groups on the right side of the face, including the forehead, together with hyperacusis. Audiology demonstrates a new right-sided sensorineural hearing loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Upper motor neuron facial weakness from a cortical stroke

questions.explanation: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is varicella zoster infection of the facial nerve, presenting with severe pain of the pinna, mouth, or face, vesicles on the pinna and external canal that erupt three to seven days after the onset of pain, hyperacusis, and sensorineural hearing loss. This combination of preceding severe pain, zoster vesicles in the ear, peripheral facial paralysis, and new sensorineural loss fits that picture.

optionExplanations.b: Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion with acute paralysis and often postauricular pain, but there are no vesicles and audiology is normal or at baseline.
optionExplanations.c: Cholesteatoma causes malodourous unilateral otorrhea and progressive conductive loss with a retraction pocket or perforation, not a vesicular eruption.
optionExplanations.d: Vestibular schwannoma produces chronic progressive hearing loss and tinnitus; facial nerve palsy is a late complication and there is no painful vesicular rash.
optionExplanations.e: A cortical upper motor neuron lesion spares the forehead, whereas all muscle groups on one side of the face are paralyzed here.

source.reference: OT23 — Table 10, Bell's Palsy vs. Ramsay Hunt Syndrome

questions.question: A 34-year-old man wakes with severe constant vertigo, vomiting, and marked imbalance that has now persisted for two days; he veers towards the left when he tries to walk. He had a febrile viral upper respiratory illness two weeks earlier. He reports no hearing change or tinnitus, and an audiogram performed today is normal. Examination shows unidirectional horizontal nystagmus with no other cranial nerve or long-tract findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Vestibular neuronitis is inflammation of the vestibular portion of cranial nerve VIII, thought to follow a viral infection, causing acute disabling vertigo with nausea, vomiting, and imbalance lasting one to five days without hearing loss, and leaving residual imbalance for days to weeks. Ataxia with veering towards the affected side is typical. The normal audiogram distinguishes it from labyrinthitis.

optionExplanations.b: Labyrinthitis involves the cochlear portion of the nerve as well, so tinnitus and hearing loss would be expected; hearing is normal here.
optionExplanations.c: Meniere's disease causes episodic attacks lasting minutes to hours with fluctuating low frequency sensorineural loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness.
optionExplanations.d: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo produces brief positional attacks of under a minute, not continuous vertigo lasting days.
optionExplanations.e: A central lesion typically gives bidirectional or vertical nystagmus with accompanying neurologic symptoms and slow compensation; his nystagmus is unidirectional and the neurological exam is otherwise normal.

questions.question: A 61-year-old woman reports two years of gradually worsening hearing in the right ear with constant right-sided tinnitus and vague unsteadiness, but no true spinning episodes. Otoscopy is normal bilaterally. Audiometry shows a right sensorineural hearing loss with a speech discrimination score that is disproportionately poor for the degree of pure tone loss, and the right acoustic stapedial reflex is absent. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: MRI of the internal auditory canal with gadolinium contrast
Non-contrast CT of the temporal bones

questions.explanation: Chronic unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus with poor speech discrimination relative to the hearing loss and an absent stapedial reflex are the classic retrocochlear pattern of acoustic neuroma, and in older patients unilateral tinnitus or sensorineural loss is acoustic neuroma until proven otherwise. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canal is the gold standard diagnostic test.

optionExplanations.b: Non-contrast CT of the temporal bones is used for cholesteatoma and bony pathology and will not reliably demonstrate a small intracanalicular schwannoma.
optionExplanations.c: Deferring imaging for six months delays diagnosis of a tumour that expands into the cerebellopontine angle and compresses the brainstem.
optionExplanations.d: Vestibular testing may show asymmetric caloric weakness as an early sign but is normal in many cases and is not the definitive test.
optionExplanations.e: Tympanometry assesses the middle ear, which is already known to be normal on otoscopy and does not explain a retrocochlear pattern.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman has nine days of nasal obstruction, thick discoloured nasal discharge, facial pain and pressure over both cheeks, and reduced sense of smell. Symptoms are severe, disturbing her sleep and preventing her from working. There is no periorbital swelling, visual change, or neurological deficit. She has no drug allergies. Which is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Intranasal corticosteroid alone, reassessing at 72 hours
CT of the paranasal sinuses before any treatment
Topical decongestant spray alone for ten days

questions.explanation: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis is diagnosed clinically when at least two PODS major symptoms are present with at least one being obstruction or purulent discharge; she has all four. Management follows symptom severity: mild to moderate disease is treated with intranasal corticosteroids alone, while severe disease is treated with intranasal corticosteroids plus antibiotics, with amoxicillin as the first-line agent.

optionExplanations.b: Intranasal corticosteroid alone with reassessment at 72 hours is the pathway for mild to moderate symptoms, not for severe disease with major functional impact.
optionExplanations.c: Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is a second-line option reserved for failure to respond to first-line therapy within 72 hours.
optionExplanations.d: CT is indicated only when complications are suspected, and there are no orbital or intracranial warning signs here.
optionExplanations.e: Decongestants are adjuvant therapy for symptomatic relief only, and prolonged topical use risks rhinitis medicamentosa.

source.reference: OT26 — Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis: Diagnosis and Management

questions.question: A 24-year-old man arrives with brisk bleeding from the right nostril that began 20 minutes ago after he picked his nose. He takes no anticoagulants and his vital signs are normal. He is seated leaning forward and firm pressure has been applied to the cartilaginous part of the nose. After a cotton pledget with topical lidocaine and decongestant, speculum examination clearly shows an oozing vessel on the anterior right septum, and bleeding continues. What is the next best step?

options.text: Cauterize the visualized bleeding point on the right septum with silver nitrate
Cauterize matching areas on both sides of the septum with silver nitrate
Place an expandable anterior nasal tampon in the right nostril
Insert a posterior balloon pack and admit for three days
Arrange transnasal endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation

questions.explanation: In epistaxis, after pressure and a first-line topical decongestant fail, the next step is cauterization with silver nitrate provided the bleeding source is adequately visualized. His bleeding point on the anterior septum is clearly seen, so chemical cautery of that single site is appropriate; both sides of the septum must not be cauterized at once because of the risk of septal perforation from loss of blood supply.

optionExplanations.b: Cauterizing both sides of the septum at one sitting risks septal perforation from loss of septal blood supply and should be avoided.
optionExplanations.c: Anterior packing with an expandable tampon is reserved for failure to achieve hemostasis with cauterization.
optionExplanations.d: Posterior packing is used when the bleeding source cannot be visualized and is likely posterior, which is not the case here.
optionExplanations.e: Arterial ligation or embolization is reserved for bleeding that persists after anterior and posterior packing have failed.

questions.question: An 18-month-old boy is brought in with two days of ear tugging, irritability, and poor sleeping. His temperature is 39.4 degrees Celsius and he is difficult to console. Otoscopy of the left ear shows a bulging tympanic membrane with marked yellow discolouration and loss of the handle of the malleus, and the membrane is immobile on pneumatic otoscopy. He has no drug allergies and no craniofacial abnormality. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: High-dose amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/d divided twice daily for 10 days
Analgesia and watchful waiting with reassessment in 24-48 hours
Referral for immediate myringotomy and tympanostomy tubes

questions.explanation: Antimicrobials are indicated in a child over 6 months with suspected acute otitis media who is moderately or severely ill, or has fever of 39 degrees Celsius or higher, or more than 48 hours of symptoms. First-line therapy without penicillin allergy is high-dose amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/d divided twice daily, and a 10-day course is used for children aged 6-24 months. This 18-month-old is markedly febrile and unsettled with a bulging, immobile, discoloured tympanic membrane.

optionExplanations.b: Watchful waiting applies to a generally healthy child over 6 months who is only mildly ill with unilateral non-severe disease and fever below 39 degrees Celsius.
optionExplanations.c: A 5-day course is recommended for most children over 2 years with uncomplicated disease; children aged 6-24 months require 10 days.
optionExplanations.d: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is used when initial therapy fails, meaning no symptomatic improvement after 2-3 days.
optionExplanations.e: Myringotomy and tubes are considered for recurrent acute otitis media with effusion at reassessment, not for a first presentation.

source.reference: OT40 — Acute Otitis Media: Management and Treatment

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl is seen six weeks after a treated episode of acute otitis media. Her parents note she turns the television up and often asks them to repeat themselves. She has no ear pain, fever, or discharge. Otoscopy shows a dull amber right tympanic membrane with a visible meniscus fluid level and air bubbles, immobile on pneumatic otoscopy. Tympanometry gives a flat tracing with no pressure peak. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observe with an audiogram to document hearing, reassessing at three months from diagnosis
A further course of oral antibiotics
An oral antihistamine with a decongestant
Immediate myringotomy with ventilation tube insertion

questions.explanation: Otitis media with effusion is fluid in the middle ear without signs or symptoms of infection, and it frequently follows acute otitis media; about 90% of children clear the fluid within three months. Management is expectant, with watchful waiting for three months from onset or from diagnosis if onset is unknown, and documentation of hearing loss with an audiogram.

optionExplanations.b: Systemic antibiotics are specifically recommended against for otitis media with effusion.
optionExplanations.c: Intranasal and systemic steroids are recommended against in this condition.
optionExplanations.d: Antihistamines and decongestants are also among the therapies recommended against for otitis media with effusion.
optionExplanations.e: Surgery is considered after the effusion and associated hearing difficulty persist beyond three months, not at six weeks.

questions.question: A 3-year-old with incomplete immunizations is brought to the emergency department after six hours of fever to 39.5 degrees Celsius, refusal to swallow, and drooling. He looks toxic and pale, sits upright leaning forward with his mouth open and tongue protruding, and has soft inspiratory stridor with slow breathing. There is no barking cough. He becomes distressed when approached. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Take him to the operating room with anesthesia and otolaryngology present to secure the airway
Use a tongue depressor to inspect the oropharynx and epiglottis
Send him to radiology for a lateral neck radiograph
Give nebulized epinephrine and dexamethasone and observe for four hours
Start intravenous ceftriaxone and observe on the ward

questions.explanation: Acute epiglottitis is a medical emergency; the toxic appearance, rapid onset, drooling, tripod posture, and inspiratory stridor without a barking cough point to supraglottic swelling. Examining the throat may precipitate laryngospasm and airway compromise, so an anesthesiologist and otolaryngologist must be present with preparations for intubation or tracheotomy before any manipulation. Securing the airway comes first, with blood and pharyngeal cultures taken after intubation.

optionExplanations.b: Instrumenting the pharynx before the airway is secured can provoke laryngospasm and complete obstruction.
optionExplanations.c: A lateral neck radiograph showing the thumb sign is only obtained if the patient is stable, and the worst place to lose an airway is during imaging.
optionExplanations.d: Nebulized epinephrine and dexamethasone treat croup, which is preceded by an upper respiratory illness with a seal-bark cough and a less toxic child.
optionExplanations.e: Antibiotics are essential but follow airway control; observing an unprotected airway in epiglottitis risks fatal obstruction.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man who swims daily has three days of right otalgia, itching, and aural fullness. Pain is aggravated by traction of the pinna and by pressure over the tragus, and it worsens with chewing. The external auditory canal is edematous and erythematous with scant otorrhea, and the tympanic membrane appears normal where it can be seen. He is afebrile. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Exostoses of the external auditory canal

questions.explanation: Otitis externa is inflammation of the external auditory canal or auricle, and acute disease presents with otalgia, itching, fullness, ear canal pain on chewing, and tenderness aggravated by traction of the pinna or pressure over the tragus, with canal edema, erythema, and possible otorrhea. Water in the ear canal from swimming is a listed risk factor. Pulling on the pinna is extremely painful in otitis externa but is usually well tolerated in otitis media.

optionExplanations.b: Pulling on the pinna is usually well tolerated in otitis media, and the findings here are canal edema and erythema rather than middle ear disease.
optionExplanations.c: Chronic otitis externa gives pruritus with an atrophic, scaly canal lining and a wide meatus, with no pain on movement of the auricle.
optionExplanations.d: Cerumen impaction causes conductive hearing loss, fullness, itching and discharge, but not an edematous erythematous canal that is tender on tragal pressure.
optionExplanations.e: Exostoses are bony protuberances of the canal that are usually an incidental finding and cause symptoms only by producing cerumen impaction or otitis externa.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has four weeks of severe left otalgia and purulent otorrhea that is refractory to two courses of topical drops. Granulation tissue is seen on the floor of the left auditory canal. He now has a new left peripheral facial nerve palsy and a temperature of 38.2 degrees Celsius. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Hospitalization for IV antibiotics with debridement and temporal bone imaging
Continue topical antimicrobial drops and keep the external auditory canal dry
Start an oral antibiotic as an outpatient and review in one week
Prescribe analgesics and treat an underlying dermatologic condition
Arrange an outpatient technetium scan and withhold treatment until the result returns

questions.explanation: Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa is osteomyelitis of the mastoid or temporal bone, occurring in elderly patients with diabetes mellitus and in the immunocompromised, most commonly caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It presents with otalgia and purulent otorrhea refractory to medical therapy plus granulation or necrotic tissue on the floor of the auditory canal, and cranial nerve palsy (most commonly CN VII) is a recognized complication. It is a medical emergency requiring hospitalization, debridement and IV antibiotics, with high resolution temporal bone CT or gadolinium-enhanced MRI.

optionExplanations.b: Topical therapy has already failed; refractory otalgia and otorrhea with granulation tissue signal skull base osteomyelitis rather than simple otitis externa.
optionExplanations.c: Oral antibiotics are used when infection spreads beyond the ear canal in ordinary otitis externa, but osteomyelitis with a cranial nerve palsy needs admission and IV therapy.
optionExplanations.d: Treating an underlying dermatologic cause applies to chronic otitis externa, not to a necrotizing infection with bone involvement.
optionExplanations.e: Technetium scanning helps demonstrate sites of osteomyelitis, but imaging must not delay hospitalization and IV antibiotics in this emergency.

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman reports 18 months of malodourous unilateral right otorrhea with progressive hearing loss and aural fullness. She had ventilation tubes as a child. Otoscopy shows a retraction pocket of the pars flaccida containing keratinous debris, with granulation tissue at its margin. The audiogram shows a conductive loss, and non-contrast CT of the temporal bones shows erosion of the ossicles. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

options.text: Mastoidectomy with tympanoplasty and ossicular reconstruction
A prolonged course of oral antibiotics
Observation with a repeat audiogram in six months

questions.explanation: Acquired cholesteatoma is frequently associated with retraction pockets in the pars flaccida or pars tensa and presents with progressive predominantly conductive hearing loss, otalgia, aural fullness, and malodourous unilateral otorrhea, often with granulation tissue on otoscopy and a history of otitis media or ventilation tubes. The associated chronic inflammatory process causes progressive destruction of surrounding bony structures, such as the ossicular erosion causing this conductive loss. Investigation is audiogram plus non-contrast CT of the temporal bones, and treatment is surgical: mastoidectomy with tympanoplasty and ossicular reconstruction.

optionExplanations.b: A ventilation tube does not remove keratinized squamous epithelium, and previous tubes are part of the history that predisposed to cholesteatoma.
optionExplanations.c: Antibiotics may temporarily reduce discharge but cannot halt the progressive bony destruction produced by cholesteatoma.
optionExplanations.d: Topical drops treat canal and middle ear infection but leave the cholesteatoma sac and its erosive potential in place.
optionExplanations.e: Observation risks ossicular and inner ear erosion, facial paralysis, mastoiditis, and intracranial complications such as meningitis.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman woke two days ago with sudden loss of hearing in the left ear accompanied by tinnitus and aural fullness. She has no vertigo, ataxia, weakness, or other focal neurological signs. Audiometry confirms a left sensorineural loss of 45 dB affecting three consecutive frequencies, with a normal right ear. History, physical examination and screening investigations reveal no underlying cause. What is the best initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss presents as sudden onset of significant SNHL, usually unilateral, with tinnitus, vertigo or aural fullness, and is idiopathic in 80-90% of cases once other causes are ruled out. When idiopathic, treatment is intratympanic or oral corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/d for 7-14 d), started within 3 d if possible and up to 14 d after onset. This woman is 2 days from onset with an audiogram confirming loss of at least 30 dB across three consecutive frequencies, so steroids should begin now.

optionExplanations.b: Antivirals treat the underlying cause only when an infectious etiology such as HSV or herpes-zoster is identified; here the workup was unremarkable.
optionExplanations.c: There is no bacterial infection to treat, and antibiotics do not alter the course of idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss.
optionExplanations.d: Gentamicin is an ototoxic aminoglycoside that damages sensory hair cells and would worsen the loss.
optionExplanations.e: Cytotoxic medication is reserved for steroid non-responders in autoimmune inner ear disease, not as initial therapy for sudden hearing loss.

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman has four consecutive springs of nasal congestion, nasal itch, watery rhinorrhea, sneezing and hyposmia, with redness, tearing and itching of the eyes. Her mother has asthma. Examination shows congested gray-blue turbinates and a transverse crease across the nasal tip. Allergen avoidance and nasal saline irrigation have not controlled her symptoms. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?
questions.explanation: Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity of the nasal mucosa presenting with nasal congestion, nasal itch, watery rhinorrhea, sneezing and hyposmia, often with allergic conjunctivitis, congested gray/blue turbinates and a nasal tip transverse crease. Seasonal disease is caused by pollen from trees, grass and ragweed. After allergen identification and avoidance and nasal saline irrigation, the intranasal corticosteroid is the mainstay of treatment.

optionExplanations.b: Decongestants are listed among other therapies only and carry the risk of rhinitis medicamentosa.
optionExplanations.c: A leukotriene receptor antagonist is an adjunct rather than the mainstay of pharmacological treatment.
optionExplanations.d: Allergen immunotherapy is reserved for patients not controlled by standard measures, not as initial drug therapy.
optionExplanations.e: Oral corticosteroids are among the other therapies and are inappropriate as first-line treatment for seasonal symptoms.

questions.question: A 32-year-old elementary school teacher has six months of gradually worsening hoarseness that is worst at the end of the day and improves over the weekend. She does not smoke or drink alcohol and has no dysphagia, weight loss or neck mass. Laryngoscopy shows bilateral symmetric lesions at the junction of the anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds of the vocal cords, with normal cord mobility. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Retention cyst of the vocal cord

questions.explanation: Vocal cord nodules are a vocal cord callus, bilateral by definition and symmetric, arising from chronic voice strain and occurring frequently in singers, children, bartenders and school teachers. Hoarseness is worst at the end of the day, and laryngoscopy shows bilateral symmetric nodules at the junction of the anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds of the cords, the point of maximal cord vibration. Primary treatment is voice rest and voice therapy with hydration and avoidance of irritants.

optionExplanations.b: A polyp is unilateral and asymmetrical, of acute onset, and typically a soft smooth pedicled or sessile lesion on the anterior one-third of one cord.
optionExplanations.c: Laryngeal carcinoma would be suggested by smoking and alcohol exposure with a mass lesion, not by symmetric bilateral lesions with normal mobility.
optionExplanations.d: Vocal cord paralysis produces a breathy voice with the affected cord in the paramedian position and impaired mobility, whereas mobility is normal here.
optionExplanations.e: A retention cyst is a solitary lesion and does not produce paired symmetric swellings at the point of maximal vibration on both cords.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man has three months of intermittent left submandibular swelling and pain that begin within minutes of starting a meal and settle over the next hour. He is afebrile with no suppurative drainage from the duct punctum. There is tenderness over the involved gland, and digital palpation of the floor of the mouth reveals a firm calculus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sialolithiasis is a ductal stone leading to chronic sialadenitis, with 80% occurring in the submandibular gland. It presents with pain and tenderness over the involved gland and intermittent swelling related to meals, and digital palpation reveals the presence of the calculus. Ultrasound is the first investigation, and if a stone is identified CT is used for localization.

optionExplanations.b: Acute sialadenitis produces acute onset pain and marked gland edema with fever, leukocytosis and suppurative drainage from the punctum, none of which are present.
optionExplanations.c: Pleomorphic adenoma is a benign salivary neoplasm presenting as a persistent mass rather than swelling that fluctuates with meals.
optionExplanations.d: Warthin's tumour is a benign parotid neoplasm, often bilateral, and does not cause a palpable ductal calculus.
optionExplanations.e: Mumps usually presents with bilateral parotid enlargement, not unilateral submandibular swelling with a palpable stone.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history is seen with a firm, painless 3 cm lateral neck mass that he first noticed eight weeks ago. It has not changed after a course of antibiotics. He is afebrile, the mass is non-tender and does not correspond to a normal neck structure such as the hyoid or a prominent carotid bulb, and there is no dental or throat pain. What is the most likely cause of this neck mass?

options.text: Metastatic malignancy from an unknown primary

questions.explanation: Any neck mass persisting for more than 2 wk should be investigated for possible neoplastic causes, once it is confirmed not to be a normal neck structure. In patients over 40 the order of prevalence of acquired causes of a neck lump is neoplastic first, then inflammatory, then congenital, the reverse of the pattern under 40. A firm, painless, persistent lateral neck mass in an older smoker fits metastatic malignancy, listed among neoplastic causes as unknown primary.

optionExplanations.b: Reactive lymphadenopathy is secondary to tonsillitis or pharyngitis and would be expected to be tender and to settle rather than persist unchanged for eight weeks.
optionExplanations.c: Branchial cleft cysts are congenital lateral neck masses, and congenital causes are the least likely group in patients over 40.
optionExplanations.d: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a congenital midline mass, whereas this lesion is lateral and arose in a man over 40.
optionExplanations.e: Sialadenitis is an inflammatory salivary gland condition with painful glandular swelling, not a painless persistent neck lump.

source.reference: OT32 — Approach to a Neck Mass

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy is brought in with heavy snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, and sleeping with his neck hyperextended. During the day he mouth breathes, is excessively sleepy, has morning headaches, and his teacher reports inattention and hyperactivity. He is otherwise healthy. Examination shows large tonsils and an open-mouthed appearance with a high arched palate. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Lateral soft tissue x-ray of the nasopharynx

questions.explanation: Sleep-disordered breathing in children is a spectrum from snoring to obstructive sleep apnea, peaking between 2 and 8 yr when the tonsils and adenoids are largest relative to the pharyngeal airway, with nighttime heavy snoring, apneic pauses and neck hyperextension and daytime mouth breathing, sleepiness, ADHD-like symptoms and morning headache. Polysomnography is the test that establishes and grades the diagnosis, with an apnea-hypopnea index above 1/h considered abnormal and severity in children graded as mild 2-4/h, moderate 6-10/h and severe more than 10/h.

optionExplanations.b: Flexible nasopharyngoscopy assesses the nasopharynx and adenoids anatomically but does not quantify apneas and hypopneas.
optionExplanations.c: A lateral soft tissue x-ray shows the adenoid shadow, and palate elevation can make the adenoid look larger, so it cannot confirm obstructive sleep apnea.
optionExplanations.d: Pulse oximetry alone does not generate an apnea-hypopnea index and is not the diagnostic study named for this presentation.
optionExplanations.e: A chest radiograph does not assess upper airway obstruction during sleep.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man has five days of sore throat, now with severe left-sided odynophagia, dysphagia, drooling and a muffled hot potato voice. Temperature is 38.7 degrees Celsius. He can barely open his mouth. There is extensive peritonsillar swelling on the left with edema of the soft palate, deviation of the uvula to the right, and tender cervical lymphadenitis. His airway is patent. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Surgical drainage by incision or needle aspiration with culture and sensitivity
Oral antibiotics alone with review in 48 hours
Warm saline irrigation and analgesia alone
Admission for IV fluids and observation without intervention

questions.explanation: Peritonsillar abscess is a cellulitis of the space behind the tonsillar capsule extending onto the soft palate and leading to abscess, most common in the 15-30 yr age group, with trismus the most reliable indicator plus uvular deviation, dysphonia, fever, drooling and extensive peritonsillar swelling. After securing the airway, treatment is surgical drainage by incision or needle aspiration with culture and sensitivity, followed by empiric oral antibiotics to a 14-day course modified by the culture results.

optionExplanations.b: Antibiotics are given after drainage and modified by culture results; medical therapy alone leaves the collection undrained and risks rupture and aspiration pneumonia.
optionExplanations.c: Elective tonsillectomy is considered after resolution of the infection and may even be deferred until after a second episode.
optionExplanations.d: Warm saline irrigation is an adjunct, not a substitute for drainage of the abscess.
optionExplanations.e: Observation risks airway obstruction, spontaneous rupture with aspiration pneumonia, and spread into the parapharyngeal or carotid space.

questions.question: An 18-month-old girl had a sudden episode of coughing and choking two hours ago while eating peanuts. She is now alert and stable with an intermittent cough. She is afebrile with a normal white blood cell count. There is a unilateral wheeze with decreased breath sounds on the right, and she has been kept NPO. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Right and left decubitus chest radiographs
Lateral soft tissue radiograph of the neck

questions.explanation: An aspirated foreign body such as a peanut is usually stuck at the right main bronchus and produces unilateral 'asthma' with wheeze and decreased breath sounds, of sudden onset and not necessarily febrile or with an elevated WBC. Any patient with a suspected foreign body should be kept NPO immediately. In a younger patient the imaging of choice is right and left decubitus chest x-rays, where lack of lung deflation while resting on the dependent side suggests a foreign body blocking a bronchus.

optionExplanations.b: Inspiratory-expiratory chest x-ray is the study for an older, stable patient who can cooperate with the breathing manoeuvre.
optionExplanations.c: A lateral neck film addresses an ingested foreign body stuck at the cricopharyngeus, whereas this child has bronchial signs.
optionExplanations.d: CT of the chest is not the described initial imaging for suspected aspirated foreign body in a young child.
optionExplanations.e: Barium swallow assesses the esophagus and is hazardous in a child who must be kept NPO pending airway endoscopy.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man with untreated caries of the lower molars has two days of worsening throat and neck pain, trismus, odynophagia and fever. He is sitting forward drooling, with erythema and swelling of the submandibular region and floor of the mouth, purulent oral discharge, dysphonia and inspiratory stridor. Oxygen saturation is 93% on room air. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: CT of the neck with contrast
Surgical drainage with extraction of the infected tooth

questions.explanation: Deep neck space infections most commonly arise from infection of the mandibular teeth in adults, often have a rapid onset and may progress to fatal complications, presenting with sore throat, trismus, dysphagia and odynophagia, swelling of the face and neck, purulent oral discharge, and stridor and dyspnea, with dysphonia and hoarseness as late findings. Ludwig's angina is the prototypical infection of the submandibular and sublingual space. Treatment order is to secure the airway first, then source control, then maximum doses of IV systemic antimicrobials.

optionExplanations.b: CT with contrast is part of the diagnostic workup, but imaging must wait because the worst place to lose an airway is during imaging.
optionExplanations.c: IV antimicrobials are essential but follow airway control and source control in a patient who already has stridor.
optionExplanations.d: Source control by drainage and tooth extraction is definitive but is performed after the airway is secured.
optionExplanations.e: A lateral cervical radiograph is a diagnostic step and does not address the immediate threat of airway loss.

questions.question: A 71-year-old woman reports a thyroid mass that has been rapidly enlarging over six weeks, with dysphagia, hoarseness, neck pain, and facial edema. She has long-standing Hashimoto's thyroiditis. She also describes fever, night sweats, chills, and 10% weight loss over six months. She has no history of differentiated thyroid carcinoma or nodular goitre. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes primary thyroid lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, as a rapidly enlarging thyroid mass with dysphagia, dyspnea, stridor, hoarseness, neck pain and facial edema accompanied by "B" symptoms, defined as fever, night sweats, chills, and weight loss of 10% in 6 months. A history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis increases the risk 60-fold, and there is a female predominance. The combination of Hashimoto's thyroiditis and B symptoms points to lymphoma rather than to anaplastic carcinoma, which is also more common in elderly women but in which 20-30% have a history of differentiated thyroid cancer or a nodular goitre mass.

optionExplanations.a: Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer but spreads by lymphatics with palpable lymph nodes, shows Orphan Annie nuclei and psammoma bodies, and carries a positive prognosis rather than a fulminant compressive presentation.
optionExplanations.b: Follicular carcinoma spreads hematogenously with far away metastases and cannot be diagnosed by FNA; it does not produce a rapidly enlarging mass with B symptoms.
optionExplanations.c: Medullary carcinoma shows amyloid on histology, may secrete calcitonin, and is associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN IIa or IIb), none of which is present here.
optionExplanations.d: Anaplastic carcinoma is also more common in the elderly with 70% in women, but 20-30% have a history of differentiated thyroid carcinoma or nodular goitre mass, and it is not linked to Hashimoto's thyroiditis or B symptoms.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman reports bilateral hearing loss that began in her early twenties and worsened during each of her two pregnancies. Her mother had the same problem. She has non-pulsatile tinnitus but no otorrhea or vertigo. Both tympanic membranes are intact apart from a faint pink blush. Audiometry shows a conductive loss with a characteristic dip at 2000 Hz. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Otosclerosis is fusion of the stapes footplate to the oval window such that it cannot vibrate; it is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, affects women more than men, and progresses during pregnancy because it is hormone responsive. It produces progressive conductive hearing loss first noticed in the teens or twenties, with a normal tympanic membrane except for a pink blush (Schwartz's sign) and a characteristic dip at 2000 Hz (Carhart's notch) on the audiogram. This woman's family history, worsening in pregnancy, drum blush and 2000 Hz dip match that description exactly.

optionExplanations.a: Cerumen impaction is the most common conductive loss in 15-50 year olds, but it obstructs the canal rather than leaving intact drums with a pink blush, and it does not run in families or progress with pregnancy.
optionExplanations.c: Presbycusis is sensorineural hearing loss associated with aging that starts in the fifth and sixth decades from hair cell degeneration, not a conductive loss in a woman in her twenties.
optionExplanations.d: Pendred is a syndrome-associated congenital sensorineural hearing loss with euthyroid goiter, the SLC26A4 gene and enlarged vestibular aqueducts, not an adult-onset conductive loss.
optionExplanations.e: Treacher-Collins is a syndrome-associated congenital hearing loss arising from first and second branchial cleft anomalies, evident from birth with craniofacial abnormality.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy is assessed for persistent left-sided hearing difficulty three months after an episode of otitis media. Tympanometry of the left ear yields a flat tracing with no pressure peak and poor tympanic membrane mobility. The measured ear canal volume is 3.2 cc. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A type B tympanogram shows no pressure peak and poor tympanic membrane mobility, which is indicative of either a middle ear effusion or a perforated tympanic membrane. The two are separated by the ear canal volume: in a type B curve, ear canal volumes of more than 2 cc in children and more than 2.5 cc in adults indicate tympanic membrane perforation or the presence of a patent ventilation tube. A flat tracing with a 3.2 cc canal volume in a 6-year-old therefore points to a perforation rather than fluid.

optionExplanations.a: A middle ear effusion also gives a flat type B curve, but the ear canal volume would be within the normal range rather than above 2 cc in a child.
optionExplanations.b: Eustachian tube dysfunction produces a type C curve with a negative pressure peak, not a flat tracing with no peak.
optionExplanations.d: With otosclerosis the peak is still at 0 mmH2O but has a lower amplitude, so the tympanogram is not flat.
optionExplanations.e: With ossicular chain discontinuity the peak is still at 0 mmH2O but has a higher amplitude, again not a flat tracing.
